1.citation: Drenoyanis, A., Raad, R., Wady, I., & Krogh, C. (2019). Implementation of an IoT Based Radar Sensor Network for Wastewater Management. Sensors, 19(2), 254. https://doi.org/10.3390/s19020254
1.intro: In this article, Drenoyanis et al. examine the design and municipal deployment of an autonomous IoT-enabled millimeter-wave radar network for real-time wastewater level tracking and overflow prevention.
1.methods: The authors designed battery-powered sensor nodes integrating 77–81 GHz FMCW millimeter-wave radar transducers, GPS, and cellular telemetry, deployed across 15 critical sewer manholes in Shoalhaven Water (Australia) over 12 months.
1.scope: Focuses on continuous water level monitoring in deep, obstructed sewer manholes with narrow inverts (150–300 mm), high humidity (95–100% RH), and confined space constraints.
1.usefulness: Highly useful to our research as it provides empirical proof that 77–81 GHz narrow-beam radar completely avoids false echoes from internal ladder rungs, step irons, and benching walls, unlike ultrasonic transducers.
1.limitations: Higher unit component cost and higher active sweep power demand compared to simple acoustic sensors, requiring strict duty-cycling (2–5 min sleep intervals) for multi-year battery autonomy.
1.conclusions: The authors conclude that 80 GHz FMCW radar provides sub-millimeter level measurement accuracy, is immune to thermal gradients and toxic sewer gas mixtures, and prevents catastrophic SSOs.
1.reflection: This study forms the foundational empirical basis for Section 2 in Paper 1, substantiating our recommendation of 77–81 GHz FMCW radar as the gold-standard non-contact level technology.

2.citation: Alshami, A., Elsayed, M., Ali, E., Eltoukhy, A. E. E., & Zayed, T. (2023). Monitoring Blockage and Overflow Events in Small-Sized Sewer Network Using Contactless Flow Sensors in Hong Kong: Problems, Causes, and Proposed Solution. IEEE Access, 11, 87131–87149. https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2023.3305275
2.intro: This paper investigates contactless open-channel flow monitoring and highlights why conventional depth-to-flow Manning equations fail during sewer blockage events.
2.methods: The authors deployed non-contact dual-radar devices combining 24 GHz microwave Doppler surface velocimeters and level sensors across small-sized gravity sewers (DN225–DN375) in Hong Kong.
2.scope: Small-diameter sewer conduits subject to severe sedimentation, grease accumulation, and tidal backwater surcharge.
2.usefulness: Crucial for our research as it mathematically and empirically demonstrates that level-only sensing fails to identify downstream blockages where water depth increases while flow velocity drops to near zero.
2.limitations: Surface velocimetry requires an empirical velocity profile integration factor (alpha approx 0.85–0.90) to estimate cross-sectional mean velocity, which fluctuates in highly turbulent or disturbed flow regimes.
2.conclusions: Direct dual-measurement of both depth and surface velocity is mandatory to detect early-stage blockages and distinguish backwater pooling from true hydraulic peak inflows.
2.reflection: Directly illuminates Section 4 of Paper 1, providing the mathematical justification for why single-parameter depth sensors cannot be used with Manning's equation during abnormal pipe conditions.

3.citation: Utepov, Y., Neftissov, A., Mkilima, T., et al. (2023). Prototyping an integrated IoT-based real-time sewer monitoring system using low-power sensors. Eastern-European Journal of Enterprise Technologies, 3(5/123), 6–23. https://doi.org/10.15587/1729-4061.2023.283393
3.intro: Utepov et al. present the prototyping, bench-testing, and embedded software architecture for low-cost, low-power sewer depth monitoring nodes.
3.methods: The authors designed edge microcomputing prototypes pairing low-power microcontrollers with optical micro-LiDAR Time-of-Flight (VL53L1X) and waterproof ultrasonic transceivers (JSN-SR04T) under simulated sewer humidity and foam conditions.
3.scope: Short-range depth sensing (0.2–4.0 m), power consumption benchmarking in sleep/active modes, and sensor housing waterproof design.
3.usefulness: Provides concrete operational data on the trade-offs between optical infrared ToF sensors and ultrasonic transducers in constrained sewer atmospheres.
3.limitations: Optical infrared ToF suffered from signal absorption on dark/turbid wastewater and condensation droplet blinding, while ultrasonic sensors showed minimum dead-band blind spots (<20 cm).
3.conclusions: Ultrasonic transducers provide superior reflection off dirty liquids compared to micro-LiDAR, but require temperature-compensated sound velocity corrections.
3.reflection: Informs the low-cost edge tier analysis in Paper 1 and justifies why acoustic and radar methods outperform optical infrared ToF in active sewer manholes.

4.citation: Sikorski, A., Solano Donado, F., & Kozdrowski, S. (2022). Cost-Efficient Coverage of Wastewater Networks by IoT Monitoring Devices. Sensors, 22(18), 6854. https://doi.org/10.3390/s22186854
4.intro: This paper develops an optimization framework for achieving maximum sewer network overflow monitoring coverage using ultra-low-cost, battery-efficient discrete IoT sentinels.
4.methods: The authors formulated a multi-objective coverage optimization model pairing zero-quiescent-power discrete float switches and tilt sensors with LoRaWAN telemetry across simulated large-scale municipal sewer networks.
4.scope: Network-wide overflow surveillance, binary surcharge alarm generation, LPWAN battery lifespan estimation (>5–10 years), and utility CAPEX minimization.
4.usefulness: Extremely useful for understanding the exact operational role of discrete binary pulse/float switches ($0$ sleep current) as high-density surcharge sentinels.
4.limitations: Binary float switches provide no rate-of-rise or diurnal flow hydrograph data until the sewage level reaches the physical switch trigger threshold.
4.conclusions: A tiered monitoring strategy combining a sparse core of continuous radar gauges with a dense swarm of binary float sentinels delivers 90%+ overflow coverage at minimal cost.
4.reflection: Substantiates Section 3 of Paper 1 by establishing the clear functional boundary between continuous depth gauges and discrete event sentinels.

5.citation: Blumensaat, F., et al. (2026). The UWO dataset -- long-term observations from a full-scale field laboratory to better understand urban hydrology at small spatio-temporal scales. Earth System Science Data, 18, 5187–5208. https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-18-5187-2026
5.intro: Blumensaat et al. present a benchmark empirical dataset collected from a full-scale urban sewer catchment equipped with high-density flow and level monitoring.
5.methods: Continuous multi-year hydrological data collection using synchronized non-contact radar level sensors, submerged area-velocity Doppler flowmeters, and raingauge networks at 1-minute resolution.
5.scope: Urban drainage dynamics, dry-weather vs wet-weather hydrographs, inflow/infiltration (I&I), and sensor data quality in hostile subterranean sewer environments.
5.usefulness: Provides the open-source empirical benchmark for evaluating continuous level and flow sensor performance under real-world hydraulic fluctuations.
5.limitations: Highlights the necessity of robust automated data validation filters to remove transient signal spikes caused by surface wave action and debris snagging.
5.conclusions: High-resolution continuous monitoring is vital to capture localized surcharge dynamics that coarse or static hydraulic models fail to predict.
5.reflection: Cited across Paper 1 as the reference field dataset for continuous sewer hydrograph and open-channel velocity dynamics.

6.citation: Bin Ali, M. T., Horoshenkov, K. V., & Tait, S. J. (2011). Rapid detection of sewer defects and blockages using acoustic-based instrumentation. Water Science and Technology, 64(8), 1700–1707. https://doi.org/10.2166/wst.2011.183
6.intro: This paper presents the development and field trial of an acoustic pulse reflectometry instrument (SewerBatt) for rapid, non-invasive sewer pipe inspection.
6.methods: Emitted low-frequency acoustic chirp pulses (0.1–5 kHz) down the sewer pipe headspace from a manhole rim and processed the reflected acoustic impulse response to detect blockages and structural defects.
6.scope: Gravity sewer pipes (DN150–DN300), inspection reaches up to 100 meters between manholes, and rapid screening without winching CCTV equipment.
6.usefulness: Proves that acoustic reflectometry can screen an entire 100-meter pipe reach in under 30 seconds to locate blockages, grease buildups, and severe collapses.
6.limitations: Line-of-sight acoustic propagation is impeded by sharp pipe bends, drop junctions, or when sewage depth exceeds 70% of pipe diameter.
6.conclusions: Acoustic pulse reflectometry achieved >85% accuracy in locating partial and total blockages rapidly from the manhole rim without entering confined spaces.
6.reflection: Forms the core evidence for Section 7 in Paper 1 regarding rapid non-invasive acoustic inspection technologies.

7.citation: See, C. H., Horoshenkov, K. V., Bin Ali, M. T., & Tait, S. J. (2021). An Acoustic Sensor for Combined Sewer Overflow Screen Condition Monitoring in a Drainage Infrastructure. Sensors, 21(2), 404. https://doi.org/10.3390/s21020404
7.intro: See et al. develop an autonomous acoustic transceiver system for continuous real-time monitoring of bar screen ragging in Combined Sewer Overflow (CSO) chambers.
7.methods: Designed an acoustic transmitter/receiver array measuring acoustic wave attenuation and frequency shifts as debris and wet wipes blind the CSO bar screen.
7.scope: CSO relief chambers, overflow bar screens, ragging detection, and remote alert generation.
7.usefulness: Directly solves the critical utility problem of fibrous ragging on overflow screens without requiring submerged probes that foul rapidly.
7.limitations: High background acoustic noise during extreme storm turbulence requires frequency notch filtering and differential thresholding algorithms.
7.conclusions: Non-contact acoustic screen monitoring successfully detected screen blinding in under 1 minute with zero submerged probe fouling.
7.reflection: Cited in Section 7 of Paper 1 as an outstanding example of non-contact acoustic sensing overcoming physical wipe ragging in sewer infrastructure.

8.citation: Yu, Y., Safari, A., Niu, X., Drinkwater, B., & Horoshenkov, K. V. (2021). Acoustic and ultrasonic techniques for defect detection and condition monitoring in water and sewerage pipes: A review. Applied Acoustics, 183, 108282. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apacoust.2021.108282
8.intro: A definitive review synthesizing acoustic reflectometry, ultrasonic guided waves, and resonance methods for non-destructive evaluation (NDE) of pipelines.
8.methods: Systematically analyzed acoustic wave propagation physics in cylindrical conduits, comparing bulk wave, guided wave, and resonance techniques across metallic, concrete, and PVC pipes.
8.scope: Pipe structural condition assessment, crack detection, wall thinning, sediment accumulation, and non-invasive transducers.
8.usefulness: Provides the wave dispersion equations and acoustic mechanics governing acoustic reflectometry and guided wave screening in partially filled sewer pipes.
8.limitations: High-frequency ultrasonic guided waves require clean acoustic coupling and attenuate rapidly through heavy external biofilm or soft sediment layers.
8.conclusions: Headspace acoustic reflectometry is optimal for operational blockage screening, whereas guided ultrasonic waves are superior for structural wall integrity and corrosion thinning.
8.reflection: Serves as the theoretical wave mechanics foundation for Section 7 of Paper 1.

9.citation: Prisutova, J., Krynkin, A., Tait, S., & Horoshenkov, K. (2022). Use of Fibre-Optic Sensors for Pipe Condition and Hydraulics Measurements: A Review. CivilEng, 3(1), 85–113. https://doi.org/10.3390/civileng3010006
9.intro: This review evaluates the application of distributed fiber-optic sensors (DTS and DAS) for sewer pipe condition assessment and continuous hydraulic monitoring.
9.methods: Examined Raman/Brillouin Distributed Temperature Sensing (DTS) and Rayleigh Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) installed along sewer pipe inverts and crowns.
9.scope: Continuous spatial profiling along kilometers of sewer pipelines, illicit connection detection, stormwater inflow (I&I) tracking, and acoustic vibration sensing.
9.usefulness: Explains how fiber-optic cables convert an entire pipeline into a continuous spatial sensor, pinpointing cold stormwater inflow and warm illegal industrial taps with meter-scale resolution.
9.limitations: High capital installation costs and vulnerability of retrofitted fiber cables to high-pressure water jetting (flushing) and mechanical rodding maintenance crews.
9.conclusions: Fiber-optic DTS provides unmatched continuous spatial tracking of thermal anomalies from cross-connections, but demands robust armored cable deployment.
9.reflection: Synthesized in Section 7 of Paper 1 to evaluate continuous distributed linear sensors versus point sensors in sewer management.

10.citation: Moradi, S., Zayed, T., & Golkhoo, F. (2019). Review on Computer Aided Sewer Pipeline Defect Detection and Condition Assessment. Infrastructures, 4(1), 10. https://doi.org/10.3390/infrastructures4010010
10.intro: A systematic review of automated Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) inspection, computer vision algorithms, and AI defect classification for sewer pipe inspection.
10.methods: Compared image processing, feature extraction, convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and robotic crawler platforms for identifying cracks, root intrusions, FOG deposits, and pipe collapses.
10.scope: Visual inspection technologies, automated defect coding (PACP / WRC standards), image quality degradation, and AI classification accuracy.
10.usefulness: Details the industry benchmark inspection modality against which online stationary sensor networks are compared for asset management and condition ranking.
10.limitations: CCTV inspection is episodic (every 5–10 years), labor-intensive, cannot operate during high flow/surcharge, and fails to provide real-time operational alerts during storm events.
10.conclusions: AI-assisted computer vision dramatically accelerates CCTV video defect scoring, but real-time network safety requires continuous online IoT sensors.
10.reflection: Incorporated in Section 7 of Paper 1 to contrast episodic visual robotic inspections with continuous permanent IoT sensory networks.

11.citation: Shi, B., Catsamas, S., Deletic, A., et al. (2022). Illicit discharge detection in stormwater drains using an Arduino-based low-cost sensor network. Water Science and Technology, 85(5), 1372–1383. https://doi.org/10.2166/wst.2022.034
11.intro: Shi et al. detail the design and deployment of an open-source, low-cost sensor network measuring electrical conductivity and temperature to detect illicit domestic sewage cross-connections in stormwater drains.
11.methods: Built Arduino-based sensor nodes equipped with toroidal/conductive electrical conductivity (EC) probes and DS18B20 temperature sensors, deployed across an urban stormwater catchment in Melbourne, Australia.
11.scope: Stormwater drains, dry-weather baseflow, sewage cross-connection detection, and low-cost hardware fabrication (<$300 USD per node).
11.usefulness: Demonstrates how electrical conductivity and diurnal temperature fluctuations serve as reliable, low-cost proxies for illicit wastewater ingress and seawater infiltration.
11.limitations: Biofilm growth and mineral scaling on direct-contact galvanic electrodes caused signal drift over 3–4 weeks, highlighting the superiority of toroidal inductive probes.
11.conclusions: High-frequency EC and temperature time series accurately flagged illicit greywater and blackwater discharges by detecting conductivity spikes during dry weather.
11.reflection: Cited in Section 5 of Paper 1 to support the analysis of electrical conductivity sensing for tracking water quality anomalies and rainwater dilution.

12.citation: Li, T., Winnel, M., Lin, H., et al. (2017). A reliable sewage quality abnormal event monitoring system. Water Research, 121, 248–257. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.watres.2017.05.040
12.intro: Li et al. develop an online multi-parameter sensor station and event-detection algorithm for tracking toxic industrial chemical dumping in municipal sewers.
12.methods: Deployed an automated online multi-sensor platform measuring pH, ORP, electrical conductivity, and turbidity coupled with principal component analysis (PCA) and support vector machines (SVM).
12.scope: Industrial catchment gravity sewers, illicit acidic/alkaline chemical dumping, WWTP protection, and real-time anomaly alarm classification.
12.usefulness: Directly informs water quality sensor selection (pH/ORP/EC) and proves how multi-sensor fusion distinguishes benign diurnal sewage fluctuations from toxic industrial shock loads.
12.limitations: Submerged electrochemical probes suffered from rapid biofouling and reference junction sulfide poisoning, requiring automated high-pressure water washing every 12 hours.
12.conclusions: Multi-parameter sensor arrays combined with machine learning successfully detected 100% of illegal chemical dumping events with false alarm rates below 2%.
12.reflection: Forms the cornerstone in Section 5 of Paper 1 for multi-parameter physicochemical sensing arrays and automated anti-fouling requirements.

13.citation: Corominas, L., et al. (2024). Profiling wastewater characteristics in intra-urban catchments using online monitoring stations. Water Science and Technology, 89(6), 1412–1426. https://doi.org/10.2166/wst.2024.069
13.intro: This empirical study investigates high-frequency online water quality monitoring across intra-urban sewer catchments to profile dynamic wastewater pollutant loads.
13.methods: Operated multiple continuous monitoring stations equipped with in-situ spectrophotometers, pH/ORP probes, and conductivity sensors across distinct urban catchment typologies (residential, commercial, industrial).
13.scope: Intra-urban sewer trunks, dynamic diurnal hydrographs, sewer catchment typology characterization, and redox potential (ORP) tracking.
13.usefulness: Demonstrates that oxidation-reduction potential (ORP) is a highly sensitive indicator of septic anaerobic conditions and sulfide generation kinetics in gravity sewers.
13.limitations: Significant capital and maintenance burden associated with operating multi-parameter spectrophotometric stations in remote manhole locations.
13.conclusions: Real-time water quality profiles revealed substantial spatial and temporal variability driven by human activity patterns and sewer hydraulic retention times.
13.reflection: Directly supports Section 5 of Paper 1 regarding the use of potentiometric ORP probes as early sentinels for septic conditions in sewer networks.

14.citation: Helm, I., Karina, G., Jalukse, L., Pagano, T., & Leito, I. (2018). Comparative validation of amperometric and optical analyzers of dissolved oxygen: a case study. Environmental Monitoring and Assessment, 190, 313. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10661-018-6692-5
14.intro: Helm et al. rigorously compare the measurement uncertainty, calibration stability, and performance of optical luminescent DO (LDO) sensors versus electrochemical Clark polarographic cells.
14.methods: Conducted extensive ISO/IEC 17025 validation protocols, drift tests, and response time experiments on optical luminescence-quenching vs. amperometric dissolved oxygen analyzers in complex water matrices.
14.scope: Dissolved oxygen (DO) monitoring (0–20 mg/L), sulfide and toxic gas poisoning, calibration drift over time, and temperature compensation.
14.usefulness: Provides rigorous experimental evidence proving why optical luminescent DO sensors are vastly superior to electrochemical Clark cells in wastewater (no electrolyte depletion, no oxygen consumption, zero sulfide poisoning).
14.limitations: Optical sensing caps suffer from photobleaching under continuous excitation light and biofouling slime accumulation, necessitating periodic wipe cleaning.
14.conclusions: Optical DO analyzers demonstrated significantly lower drift (<1% over 3 months), required zero flow dependence, and were completely unaffected by H2S poisoning.
14.reflection: Directly provides the comparative scientific evidence in Section 5 of Paper 1 for recommending optical luminescent DO over electrochemical sensors in sewer networks.

15.citation: Lepot, M., Torres, A., Hofer, T., et al. (2016). Calibration of UV/Vis spectrophotometers: A review and comparison of different methods to estimate TSS and total and dissolved COD concentrations in sewers, WWTPs and rivers. Water Research, 101, 519–534. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.watres.2016.05.070
15.intro: A definitive review and methodological evaluation of in-situ UV-Vis spectrophotometry for real-time estimation of Total Suspended Solids (TSS) and Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD) in wastewater.
15.methods: Evaluated single-wavelength, multi-wavelength, and full-spectrum (200–750 nm) chemometric calibration models (PLS, PCR, SVM) across field data collected from municipal sewers and WWTPs.
15.scope: In-situ UV-Vis spectrometry, optical path length selection (1–5 mm for raw sewage), turbidity compensation, and organic matter surrogacy.
15.usefulness: Critical for understanding optical absorbance physics (Beer-Lambert law), turbidity cross-interference, and site-specific chemometric calibration algorithms for real-time organic load tracking.
15.limitations: Raw wastewater requires short optical path lengths (1–2 mm) to prevent light saturation; mechanical wiper cleaning or ultrasonic cavitation is mandatory to prevent window fouling.
15.conclusions: Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression over multi-wavelength UV-Vis spectra yields robust real-time COD (R2 > 0.90) and TSS proxies once site-specific turbidity compensation is applied.
15.reflection: Serves as the central scientific reference in Section 6 of Paper 1 for UV-Vis spectrophotometric organic load and solids monitoring in sewers.

16.citation: Carstea, E. M., Bridgeman, J., Baker, A., & Reynolds, D. M. (2016). Fluorescence spectroscopy for wastewater monitoring: A review. Water Research, 95, 205–219. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.watres.2016.03.021
16.intro: This review evaluates the application of 2D excitation-emission matrix (EEM) fluorescence spectroscopy for real-time organic characterization and biological oxygen demand (BOD5) monitoring in wastewater.
16.methods: Synthesized optical fluorophore mechanics across sewage matrices, focusing on Protein-like Peak T (Tryptophan, ex 280 nm, em 350 nm) and Peak B (Tyrosine) vs. Humic-like Peaks A and C.
16.scope: Optical fluorescence spectroscopy, instantaneous biochemical oxygen demand (BOD5) surrogacy, microbial activity tracking, and inner-filter effect corrections.
16.usefulness: Provides the scientific justification for using Tryptophan Peak T fluorescence as an instantaneous optical proxy for the standard 5-day BOD5 laboratory test in sewer catchments.
16.limitations: High sample absorbance and suspended solids cause inner-filter attenuation and scattering, requiring optical turbidity correction and temperature compensation.
16.conclusions: Tryptophan Peak T fluorescence correlates exceptionally well with labile organic matter (R2 > 0.85–0.95) and provides instantaneous feedback on raw sewage microbial strength.
16.reflection: Directly provides the theoretical and empirical foundation for Section 6 of Paper 1 on optical fluorescence spectroscopy for real-time organic load monitoring.

17.citation: Tan, E. X., Anastasi, A., & Chandra, S. (2022). Electrochemical detection of nitrate, nitrite and ammonium for on-site water quality monitoring. Current Opinion in Electrochemistry, 32, 100926. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.coelec.2021.100926
17.intro: Tan et al. review electrochemical sensor technologies and ion-selective electrodes (ISEs) for on-site nutrient detection (NH4+, NO2-, NO3-) in wastewater.
17.methods: Evaluated potentiometric ion-selective field-effect transistors (ISFETs), PVC membrane ISEs, and amperometric nutrient sensors for real-time nitrogen speciation in water.
17.scope: Electrochemical nutrient sensing, ammonium and nitrate tracking, ionic cross-interference (K+, Cl-), and solid-state membrane longevity.
17.usefulness: Outlines the working mechanisms and limitations of electrochemical nutrient probes deployed for in-situ sewer monitoring and illicit industrial waste tracking.
17.limitations: Potassium ions (K+) severely interfere with ammonium (NH4+) ionophore membranes, requiring concurrent potassium compensation sensors; membrane fouling limits field deployment life to 1–3 months without maintenance.
17.conclusions: Solid-state polymeric ISEs with dynamic interference compensation algorithms provide feasible on-site nutrient tracking, though routine recalibration remains necessary.
17.reflection: Synthesized in Section 5 of Paper 1 to analyze nutrient sensor performance and electrochemical cross-interference challenges.

18.citation: Sonawane, J. M., Ezugwu, C. I., & Ghosh, P. C. (2020). Microbial Fuel Cell-Based Biological Oxygen Demand Sensors for Monitoring Wastewater: State-of-the-Art and Practical Applications. ACS Sensors, 5(8), 2297–2316. https://doi.org/10.1021/acssensors.0c01299
18.intro: A state-of-the-art review on Microbial Fuel Cell (MFC) biosensors for continuous, self-powered biological oxygen demand (BOD) and toxicity monitoring in wastewater.
18.methods: Analyzed exoelectrogenic biofilm kinetics (e.g., Geobacter, Shewanella) on conductive anode electrodes where extracellular electron transfer produces electrical current proportional to biodegradable organic substrate concentration.
18.scope: Bioelectrochemical biosensors, real-time BOD measurement (5–500 mg/L), heavy metal toxicity shock detection, and self-powered bio-battery operation.
18.usefulness: Explains the operational physics of bioelectrochemical biosensors that directly measure biologically assimilable organic matter in sewers without chemical reagents.
18.limitations: Biofilm metabolic lag (10–30 min response time), substrate saturation at high COD concentrations, sensitivity to wastewater temperature fluctuations, and biofilm vulnerability to extreme toxic chemical flushes.
18.conclusions: MFC biosensors deliver a linear electrical current response for low-to-medium BOD concentrations while serving as a continuous early-warning system for microbial toxic shocks.
18.reflection: Directly forms Section 6 of Paper 1 on biological and bioelectrochemical biosensing in wastewater networks.

19.citation: Pandey, S. K., Kim, K.-H., & Tang, K.-T. (2012). A review of sensor-based methods for monitoring hydrogen sulfide. TrAC Trends in Analytical Chemistry, 32, 87–99. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trac.2011.08.008
19.intro: Pandey et al. provide a comprehensive analysis of sensor-based techniques for detecting and quantifying hydrogen sulfide (H2S) in gaseous and liquid phases.
19.methods: Systematically compared electrochemical amperometric cells, metal oxide semiconductors (MOS), optical absorbance/fluorescence, and conductometric gas sensors for H2S quantification.
19.scope: H2S sensing principles, detection limits (ppb to ppm levels), response times, cross-sensitivity to humidity and volatile organic compounds (VOCs).
19.usefulness: Establishes the chemical kinetics and sensor transducer principles governing biogenic sulfuric acid generation, odor nuisance, and concrete crown corrosion in sewer headspace.
19.limitations: Standard MOS sensors operate at high heater temperatures (200–400°C) requiring high power; electrochemical gas cells suffer from electrolyte dry-out in dry seasons and condensation flooding in 100% RH sewers.
19.conclusions: Electrochemical gas sensors offer the best balance of low power consumption and ppb-to-ppm sensitivity for battery-powered sewer IoT monitoring, provided moisture-permeable membranes are utilized.
19.reflection: Provides the theoretical and chemical foundation in Section 5 of Paper 1 for headspace H2S sensing and sewer asset preservation.

20.citation: Pacheco Fernández, M., Despot, D., & Barjenbruch, M. (2021). Comparison of H2S Gas Sensors: A Sensor Management Procedure for Sewer Monitoring. Sustainability, 13(19), 10779. https://doi.org/10.3390/su131910779
20.intro: This empirical study evaluates the field performance and longevity of multiple commercial electrochemical H2S gas sensors deployed inside municipal sewer manholes.
20.methods: Field-tested four different electrochemical H2S sensor units under harsh real sewer conditions (continuous 95–100% RH, H2S peaks up to 500 ppm, biogenic sulfuric acid) over 6 months, developing a utility sensor management procedure.
20.scope: Manhole headspace gas monitoring, sensor calibration decay, condensation blinding, electrolyte acidification, and operational lifetime.
20.usefulness: Directly informs utility sensor maintenance schedules and documents the real-world lifespan of electrochemical gas sensors in aggressive sewer atmospheres.
20.limitations: Sensors experienced severe signal drift and zero-baseline drift after 3–4 months due to acid condensation on membrane pores and electrolyte saturation.
20.conclusions: Developed a standardized maintenance protocol indicating that electrochemical H2S sensors in sewer headspaces require recalibration every 2–3 months and membrane replacement every 6–12 months.
20.reflection: Directly cited in Section 5 and Section 8 of Paper 1 to substantiate the maintenance intervals and failure modes of sewer gas monitoring instrumentation.

21.citation: Despot, D., Pacheco Fernández, M., & Barjenbruch, M. (2021). Comparison of Online Sensors for Liquid Phase Hydrogen Sulphide Monitoring in Sewer Systems. Water, 13(13), 1876. https://doi.org/10.3390/w13131876
21.intro: This research paper compares direct liquid-phase in-situ dissolved sulfide sensors with indirect headspace gas sensors for real-time sewer corrosion and chemical dosing management.
21.methods: Evaluated submerged UV spectrophotometric probes measuring dissolved bisulfide ions (HS- at 230 nm) directly in raw sewage in parallel with headspace H2S gas analyzers and chemical dosing pumps.
21.scope: Liquid-phase sulfide speciation (H2S <=> HS- + H+), pH dependence, real-time iron salt / nitrate dosing control, and optical biofilm fouling.
21.usefulness: Proves that liquid-phase UV bisulfide measurement provides immediate feedback for chemical dosing (preventing expensive over-dosing) long before H2S gas volatilizes into the headspace.
21.limitations: Submerged UV probes experience rapid biological biofilm growth on optical windows within 48 hours, requiring automated mechanical wiping or compressed air cleaning.
21.conclusions: In-situ liquid HS- monitoring allows precise, closed-loop chemical dosing control, reducing utility chemical costs by up to 30% compared to reactive gas-phase monitoring.
21.reflection: Serves as the primary evidence in Section 5 of Paper 1 for liquid-phase dissolved sulfide sensing and real-time corrosion mitigation dosing.

22.citation: Lopez-Ramirez, G. A., & Aragon-Zavala, A. (2023). Wireless Sensor Networks for Water Quality Monitoring: A Comprehensive Review. IEEE Access, 11, 95120–95142. https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2023.3308905
22.intro: A comprehensive review investigating subterranean and surface wireless sensor network (WSN) topologies, telemetry protocols, and packaging architectures for water infrastructure.
22.methods: Compared RF propagation loss, antenna radiation patterns, communication protocols (LoRaWAN, NB-IoT, ZigBee), and energy harvesting mechanisms across subterranean manholes and water distribution assets.
22.scope: Subterranean RF attenuation through cast-iron and reinforced concrete manhole covers (20–40 dB loss), IP68 submersible enclosures, and LPWAN network topology.
22.usefulness: Directly informs the electronic packaging, telemetry selection, and antenna placement strategies necessary to transmit sensor data reliably from underground sewers to cloud servers.
22.limitations: Heavy cast-iron manhole covers severely attenuate high-frequency radio signals, requiring manhole-rim slot antennas or non-metallic composite cover replacements.
22.conclusions: Sub-GHz LPWAN protocols (LoRaWAN 868/915 MHz and NB-IoT Band 8/20) provide the highest penetration and range for subterranean sewer monitoring nodes.
22.reflection: Forms the foundational technical reference for Section 8 of Paper 1 regarding subterranean telemetry, radio path loss, and edge node packaging.

23.citation: de Camargo, E. T., et al. (2023). Low-Cost Water Quality Sensors for IoT: A Systematic Review. Sensors, 23(9), 4424. https://doi.org/10.3390/s23094424
23.intro: A systematic review exploring low-cost sensing hardware, open-source microcontrollers, and edge processing architectures for IoT water monitoring.
23.methods: Systematically categorized and benchmarked low-cost sensors for pH, turbidity, conductivity, temperature, and dissolved oxygen paired with low-power microcontrollers (ESP32, Arduino, ARM Cortex).
23.scope: Edge microcomputing, analog-to-digital sensor conditioning, sleep-mode power management, calibration protocols, and total cost of ownership.
23.usefulness: Provides clear cost-performance curves and design blueprints for developing scalable, low-cost edge sensing nodes for high-density sewer monitoring deployments.
23.limitations: Low-cost consumer-grade sensor components suffer from higher thermal drift and lower chemical resistance, requiring intelligent firmware filtering and baseline correction.
23.conclusions: Low-cost edge sensor nodes achieve acceptable operational accuracy when paired with digital temperature compensation and edge-computed drift correction algorithms.
23.reflection: Directly supports Section 8 of Paper 1 regarding low-cost edge processing, duty cycling, and scalable sensor node architectures.

24.citation: Crowley, G, Tait, S, Panoutsos, G, Speight, V & Esnaola, I 2025, ‘Information-theoretic sensor placement for large sewer networks’, Water Research, vol. 268, p. 122718.
24.intro: In this paper, the authors approach Optimal Sensor placement in Sewage network from an Information theory discipline and proposes a framework for optimising sensor placement.
24.methods: The author formulates the problem as mutual information maximisation problem and develop a one-step modified greedy algorithm to make the computation feasible.
24.scope: The framework was applied to two real sewer networks, one in southern England containing 479 nodes and 567 links, and one in Bellinge, Denmark, containing 1,020 nodes and 1,015 links.
24.usefulness: The paper provides a quantitative, information-theoretic approach for selecting monitoring locations as well as all data required to verify their findings.
24.limitations: The formulation makes a lot of assumptions about the representations of network states and sensor noise and the evaluation metrics do not directly reflect real world improvement
24.conclusions: The authors conclude that the one-step modified greedy algorithm generally produces better sensor placements than the other heuristic approaches considered, while mutual information provides a suitable basis for designing monitoring infrastructure in large sewer networks.
24.reflection: This work provides strong insights on how to model the OSP problem using information theory but evaluation metrics do not reflect indication of real world performance.

25.citation: Wang, S, Xu, K & Zhou, Y 2024, ‘Cost-effective sensor placement optimization for large-scale urban sewage surveillance’, Sustainable Cities and Society, vol. 103, p. 105250.
25.intro: This paper investigates optimal sensor placement for large-scale urban sewage surveillance, with particular emphasis on cost-effective monitoring during pandemics. The authors recognise that sewage networks can provide city-scale information about community health, but determining effective sensor locations becomes increasingly difficult as network size and complexity increase.
25.methods: The authors formulate sensor placement as a multi-objective optimisation problem involving competing objectives such as monitoring coverage and sensing cost. A connectivity-based objective evaluation method is developed for large directed sewage networks and incorporated into the NSGA-II evolutionary optimisation algorithm. The resulting sensor placement strategies are compared with human-generated placement heuristics.
25.scope: The proposed approach is evaluated using a real-world sewage network in Tuen Mun, Hong Kong, serving more than 500,000 residents. The study focuses on city-scale sewage surveillance and examines how computational optimisation can generate sensor placement plans for large and topologically complex networks.
25.usefulness: The paper is highly useful for understanding multi-objective OSP in large sewer networks. It demonstrates how network connectivity can be incorporated into the objective function and provides a real-world benchmark dataset and computational approach that can support further research into large-scale sewage sensor placement.
25.limitations: The approach depends heavily on the representation of network connectivity and the objectives selected for the optimisation. Although the study demonstrates improved performance compared with human placement heuristics, the optimisation objectives are proxies for surveillance effectiveness and may not fully capture real-world factors such as sensor reliability, maintenance requirements, hydraulic uncertainty or sampling variability.
25.conclusions: The authors conclude that the proposed optimisation approach can efficiently generate cost-effective sensor placement plans for large-scale sewage surveillance. The optimised solutions significantly outperform human placement heuristics, demonstrating the value of computational intelligence and network-based optimisation for city-scale sensing.
25.reflection: This paper is particularly relevant to my research because it demonstrates how OSP can be formulated as a multi-objective problem rather than optimising a single measure. The use of NSGA-II is also useful for understanding how evolutionary optimisation can handle the competing objectives and computational complexity associated with large sewer networks.

26.citation: Salem, AK & Abokifa, AA 2024, ‘Sensor Placement Optimization in Sewer Networks: Machine Learning–Based Source Identification Approach’, Journal of Water Resources Planning and Management, vol. 150, no. 11.
26.intro: In this paper, the authors address optimal sensor placement in sewer networks from the perspective of improving contaminant source identification. The paper proposes a framework that combines machine learning with optimisation to determine sensor locations that improve the ability to identify the source of contamination events.
26.methods: The authors develop a multilayer perceptron (MLP) model to predict contaminant concentrations at potential sensor locations. The predictions are then incorporated into a genetic algorithm that searches for sensor configurations which maximise source-identification performance. The framework considers both observability and reliability of source identification.
26.scope: The proposed framework was demonstrated using a real-life midsize sewer network. Multiple scenarios were investigated, including the optimal placement of a single sensor, multiple sensors, and the extension of an existing sensor network. The study evaluates the trade-off between observability and reliability under different sensor configurations.
26.usefulness: The paper is particularly useful for understanding how machine learning can be integrated directly into the sensor placement optimisation process. It demonstrates that OSP does not necessarily need to optimise simple network properties such as coverage, but can instead optimise the performance of a downstream task such as contamination source identification.
26.limitations: The framework relies on a machine learning model whose predictions influence the resulting sensor placement, meaning that inaccuracies or limitations in the source-identification model may propagate into the optimisation results. The study also focuses on a midsize sewer network, so the scalability and generalisation of the approach to much larger networks require further investigation.
26.conclusions: The authors conclude that integrating machine learning-based source identification with sensor placement optimisation provides a practical approach for improving wastewater surveillance. The results demonstrate a trade-off between sensor observability and source-identification reliability, highlighting the importance of considering both measures when designing a sensor network.
26.reflection: This work provides useful insight into task-oriented sensor placement, where the value of a sensor is determined by how well it supports a specific objective rather than simply how much of the network it covers. For my research, it demonstrates how machine learning could be incorporated into an OSP framework for contamination detection and source identification.

27.citation: Moradi, M, Najafi, M, Lin, Z & Pan, H 2025, ‘Advancing sensor network optimization and data analytics for smart wastewater and stormwater collection systems: An overview’, Proceedings of the Pipelines 2025 Conference, pp. 463–474.
27.intro: This paper provides an overview of the role of sensor networks, optimisation and data analytics in developing smart wastewater and stormwater collection systems. Rather than proposing a single sensor placement algorithm, the authors discuss how sensing, data analysis and optimisation can be combined to improve the monitoring and management of underground water infrastructure.
27.methods: The authors conduct an overview of existing approaches related to sensor network optimisation and data analytics for wastewater and stormwater collection systems. The work considers the relationship between sensing technologies, network monitoring, data-driven analysis and optimisation, identifying opportunities for integrating these components into smart infrastructure systems.
27.scope: The paper covers sensor network applications in wastewater and stormwater collection systems, with emphasis on monitoring, optimisation and data analytics. It considers the broader transition from conventional infrastructure management towards data-driven and smart collection systems.
27.usefulness: The paper is useful for establishing the broader context of optimal sensor placement within smart wastewater management. It helps connect OSP with related areas such as IoT sensing, data analytics, machine learning and infrastructure management, and therefore provides a useful foundation for identifying research gaps and potential future directions.
27.limitations: As an overview rather than a focused experimental study, the paper does not provide a single comprehensive optimisation framework that can be directly applied to a specific sewer network. The discussion also depends on the availability and quality of sensing and infrastructure data, which can vary considerably between utilities.
27.conclusions: The authors highlight the importance of integrating sensor network optimisation and data analytics to advance smart wastewater and stormwater collection systems. The combination of sensing technologies with advanced analytical and optimisation methods can enable more informed monitoring and infrastructure management.
27.reflection: This work helps place optimal sensor placement within the larger concept of smart wastewater infrastructure. It is particularly relevant to my research because it shows that sensor placement should be considered together with data analytics and operational objectives rather than as an isolated optimisation problem.

28.citation: Moradi, M & Najafi, M 2026, ‘Risk-Driven Sensor Placement in Sewer Networks: A Descriptive–Predictive–Prescriptive Framework’, Water, vol. 18, no. 15, p. 1901.
28.intro: This paper proposes a risk-driven approach to optimal sensor placement in sewer networks by connecting machine-learning-based failure prediction with sensor placement optimisation. The authors introduce a Descriptive–Predictive–Prescriptive Sensor-Placement (DPP-SP) framework that aims to place sensors where they can provide the greatest coverage of network risk.
28.methods: The proposed framework first reconstructs the sewer network topology using GIS data and develops machine-learning models to predict pipe failure risk. Random Forest, XGBoost and multilayer perceptron models are evaluated, with Random Forest providing the strongest predictive performance. The resulting pipe-level risk scores are then incorporated into a maximum weighted-coverage sensor placement problem. Greedy, genetic algorithm and tabu search methods are used to identify sensor locations that maximise risk-weighted coverage.
28.scope: The framework was applied to a large sewer system containing 33,349 pipes. The study evaluates the existing configuration of 48 monitoring stations and investigates optimised configurations with different sensor budgets. It also examines the sensitivity of sensor placement performance to the assumed upstream detection radius.
28.usefulness: The paper provides a strong example of integrating machine learning and optimisation into an end-to-end sensor placement framework. Its risk-weighted objective is particularly useful because it moves beyond treating all parts of a sewer network as equally important and instead prioritises locations associated with greater predicted failure risk.
28.limitations: The results depend on the quality of the available failure data, GIS network representation and machine-learning predictions. The utility data used in the study are confidential and cannot be publicly redistributed. In addition, the reported coverage ceiling is influenced by the candidate sensor locations and assumed detection radius, meaning that the results may not directly generalise to other sewer networks.
28.conclusions: The authors conclude that the DPP-SP framework can substantially improve risk coverage without necessarily increasing the number of sensors. Using the existing budget of 48 sensors, the optimised configuration achieved substantially greater risk coverage than the existing arrangement. The study also identifies detection radius and network fragmentation as important factors affecting achievable coverage.
28.reflection: This paper is highly relevant to my research because it demonstrates how an OSP problem can be formulated around a practical infrastructure objective: reducing monitoring risk. The integration of machine-learning-based risk prediction with optimisation provides a potential direction for developing a multi-stage or data-driven sensor placement framework.

29.citation: Ma, Y., Guo, T. and Wang, Y., 2025, 'Optimal Arrangement Strategy of IoT Sensors in Urban Drainage Networks: A Review', Applied Sciences, vol. 15, article 4976.
29.intro: In this review, the authors examine how IoT sensors are used to monitor urban drainage networks. They note that while real-time sensor monitoring has expanded rapidly with the growth of IoT technology, the complex layouts and large number of nodes in drainage pipe networks still make it hard to decide where sensors should actually be placed.
29.methods: The authors aim to develop a general framework for optimally placing IoT sensors in drainage networks, classify the parameters monitored at different points in the system, and compare the strengths and weaknesses of various placement optimisation theories. They conducted a structured literature review, searching Web of Science with keywords related to time, technology, network type and theme. The search yielded 189 papers, screened down to 96 studies, with additional literature drawn from related hydraulic networks such as water supply and river systems.
29.scope: The review focuses on two main areas of monitoring: assessing operational status via hydraulic parameters (flow rate, water level, flow velocity), and identifying abnormal events through water-quality-based pollutant tracing and flood or overflow hotspot monitoring. It also examines five categories of placement theory - engineering experience, information theory, statistical and cluster analysis, complex network theory, and observability theory - along with methods for evaluating a completed sensor scheme.
29.usefulness: This article is useful for my research as it gives a broad overview of different methods used to optimise sensor placement in drainage networks, helping me understand the range of approaches available before deciding which is best suited to SA Water's network.
29.limitations: The authors acknowledge there is still no standardised process for quantitatively evaluating monitoring schemes, and current layout methods may not actually be optimal. Entropy-based methods tend to push sensors toward the edges of a network rather than where they would be most practically useful, and cluster-based methods require the number of clusters to be set in advance, which can overlook the value of individual monitoring points. Relatively few studies have applied observability theory specifically to hydraulic monitoring in drainage networks, a gap that aligns well with what I am working on.
29.conclusions: The authors conclude that sensor placement should aim to maximise useful, non-redundant information based on the monitoring objective, and that combining multiple optimisation theories into hybrid strategies is a promising direction. They suggest future research should move toward dynamic optimisation, using phased sensor deployment and feedback iteration to improve accuracy and objectivity of network design.
29.reflection: This review has given me a broad overview of the different approaches used for optimal sensor placement in drainage networks, useful at this early stage of my literature review. It will help guide how I evaluate and compare other sources as I continue researching methods suited to SA Water's network.
